extracted.intended_audience: writers and readers of moral and satirical essays; educated periodical readership
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on composing moral/satirical periodical essays: how to choose targets for satire, how to characterize people fairly, and persuasive strategies (use of authorities, framing intentions/actions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire should target corrigible faults and discriminate
rubrics_metrics.description: A Satyr should expose nothing but what is corrigible, and make a due Discrimination between those who are, and those who are not the proper Objects of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'levelling Satyrs' that 'expose the Sex in general' or attack an entire class with superficial strokes of wit (examples: Juvenal, Boileau). Satire's purpose is correction, not wholesale condemnation; pick targets whose faults can be amended and distinguish individuals from a condemning generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray diversity of characters and do justice to virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet has shewn a great Penetration in this Diversity of Female Characters, he has avoided the Fault ... of exposing the Sex in general, without doing Justice to the valuable Part of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting a class (e.g., women, men, social types), show varied characters and acknowledge admirable qualities alongside vices. Anti-pattern: reducing a whole sex or group to one satirical caricature; instead provide balanced, discriminating portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use respected authorities and examples for moral persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: When I employ myself upon a Paper of Morality, I generally consider how I may recommend the particular Virtue which I treat of, by the Precepts or Examples of the ancient Heathens; by that Means, if possible, to shame those who have greater Advantages of knowing their Duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To persuade a mixed audience (including those who distrust certain sources), cite examples and precepts from authorities likely to command their respect (e.g., pagan philosophers) so the lesson reaches readers who might dismiss overtly religious appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame moral arguments by distinguishing intentions and actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Cast all our Actions under the Division of such as are in themselves either Good, Evil, or Indifferent. If we divide our Intentions after the same Manner, and consider them with regard to our Actions, we may discover that great Art and Secret of Religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the tripartite scheme (actions: good/evil/indifferent; intentions likewise) to analyze moral cases: show how a good intention can ennoble indifferent acts or mitigate evil acts, and how evil intentions corrupt good actions. Employ scriptural, philosophical, and historical examples (e.g., Socrates) to illustrate the framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use human appetites/instincts as rhetorical premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Since Nature ... does nothing in vain ... Futurity is the proper Object of the Passion so constantly exercis'd about it; and this Restlessness in the present ... appears to me ... as a kind of Instinct or natural Symptom which the Mind of Man has of its own Immortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing metaphysical or moral claims (e.g., immortality), appeal to observable human desires and tendencies (appetite for knowledge, appetite to duration) as presumptive evidence; show how ordinary instincts cohere with your thesis to strengthen persuasive force.

rubrics_metrics.name: To influence the powerful: be considerable or agreeable
rubrics_metrics.description: There are but two Ways of doing any thing with great People, and those are by making your self either considerable or agreeable: The former is not to be attained but by finding a Way to live without them, or concealing that you want them; the latter is only by falling into their Taste and Pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As practical/social advice (useful for character depiction or moral counsel), present two strategies for dealing with patrons: cultivate independent worth (or the appearance of it) or adapt to their tastes. Note the ethical/servile implications of 'being agreeable'—it often requires adopting another's preferences rather than cultivating intrinsic qualities.
